Q: How to calculate len size from unsigned char* in C++20? A:

Yes, unsigned char, signed char, and char are all exactly one byte large, so s.size() gets you the size in bytes of your string.

The subsequent two lines are unnecessary, and it's also worth noting some problems:

  • std::u8string(s.begin(), s.end()).data() is taking the pointer to a temporary char8_t array, so that pointer immediately dangles. Also, calling the constructor of std::u8string like that doesn't do any transcoding. Your original string already needs to be UTF-8, otherwise this doesn't make much sense.
  • There is no reason to use std::ssize instead of std::size here. You're trying to get a std::size_t result anyway, and std::size does that directly.

Assuming your goal is to "get the UTF-8 bytes" of the std::string, the proper way to write it looks like:

std::string s = "...";
std::span<const unsigned char> ut8_bytes(
  reinterpret_cast<const unsigned char*>(s.data()),
  s.size()
);

This obviously assumes that your string literals are UTF-8 encoded though. If not, you'll need to transcode s to UTF-8 before taking the bytes.

Q: C read() and write() while loop A:

My main concern is how nbajt value is changing.

nbajt is increased by count byte each iteration, where count is:

ssize_t read(int fd, void buf[count], size_t count);

read() attempts to read up to count bytes from file descriptor fd into the buffer starting at buf.

Q: Is it possible to get a programming job with just a certificate A:

Yes it is possible. (Bill Gates dropped out of Harvard ... so anything is possible ... for some people.)

But (IMO) it is not a good way to proceed. You are better off getting a proper degree or diploma in software engineering, data analysis.

If you go the certificate route, you likely to be limited in the employers who will even look at your job application. (Especially if you >just< have a certificate.) So you are likely to start off in a job with poor pay and poor prospects ... and probably a poor workplace / programming culture, where you are likely to pick up lots of bad habits. It could be difficult getting over that hurdle.

But it all depends on what programming opportunities there are in your >local< economy, and we have no idea what that is / will be like. And you could "know someone who knows someone" who will give you your first programming job. Stuff like that happens.

Q: Using Visual Studio 2026 with Docker Desktop and Podman per environment A:

Synchronized settings for Visual Studio are turned on by default. You can turn off synchronization by unchecking Synchronize settings across devices and installs on this machine options in Tools > Options > Environment > Accounts page. You can refer to this docs page.

The default setting for container runtime is Auto which means it must be able to detect currently active container runtime. As per this docs page, you can run and manage containers using the Podman CLI directly from VS and Podman CLI must be started before VS is launched. If it still doesn't work, I don't have any clue and the only option I see is using Docker Desktop at home.
